claims.text: Two-phase coexistence simulations can accurately predict melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
Interface pinning simulations can accurately predict melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
Two-phase coexistence or interface pinning substantially reduces computational expense relative to full ab initio free-energy methods.
The refractory materials are modeled near the melting point, initially close to the solid phase.
A two-phase coexistence or interface pinning simulation directly samples the solid-liquid phase boundary.
Constant-energy or constant-pressure ensembles can permit coexistence of solid and liquid phases near the melting temperature.
The relevant structural mediator is the interface between coexisting solid and liquid states.
Direct sampling of the solid-liquid interface reduces the need for full thermodynamic integration.
Direct interface sampling efficiently captures the free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases.
The proposed method enables extraction of the melting temperature.
The proposed method enables extraction of the entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The proposed method enables extraction of the volume change at the melting point.
The proposed method will produce melting properties comparable in accuracy to full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The proposed method will require only a fraction of the computational cost of full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The reduced computational cost makes the proposed method suitable for high-throughput studies.
The efficiency and accuracy of the method may decline in systems with complex or slow-moving phase boundaries.
The performance of the method requires verification across different refractory materials.
Exact quantitative differences between the proposed and baseline approaches have not been established across different materials.
